passage: I'm Darshan, and I only noticed this last term. In the hostel mess in Pune, when someone made a joke about Biharis, I suddenly felt very Bihari, more than I ever had back in Patna. In the lab, arguing about circuit design with Madhav, I was just an engineer; nobody's hometown mattered. And on match nights in the common room I was a cricket fan, yelling at the screen with guys from five states. Same week, same me, three different people stepping forward depending on who was around. At first it confused me. Then it helped. When the mess joke stung, I remembered I'm also the boy who fixed Madhav's circuit, and the one who predicted Sunday's batting collapse. No single label gets to be the whole of me.

qa.a: Madhav's circuit.

passage: College counsellor's note, 7 March. Written by Kashish. Avni, nineteen, came in upset after a clash in a group project. She said that in her Gujarati cultural society she is proud to be "the Gujarati girl," in the coding club she is "the only woman who stays till midnight," and in her dance troupe she is just "Avni who's always late." This week a teammate joked that girls in tech "just do the slides," and for two days she felt like nothing but the woman in tech, and angry. We talked about how different parts of her take the lead depending on the company she is in. She listed five identities on a sheet. By the end she was smiling a little: "He saw one of me. There are four others." She will raise the remark with the project lead, and see me again next week.

qa.q: How many identities did Avni list on the sheet?
qa.a: Five identities.

qa.q: What does Avni's 'He saw one of me. There are four others' suggest she now feels?
qa.a: She feels less trapped by the teammate's remark, seeing it touched only one part of who she is.

qa.q: What next steps did Avni and Kashish agree on?
qa.a: Avni will raise the remark with the project lead and see Kashish again next week.

qa.q: How might Avni's dance troupe see her, compared with the coding club?
qa.a: The troupe knows her as 'Avni who's always late', a light everyday identity, while the club sees her as the woman who stays till midnight.

grounding: A student learns that different identities come forward in different settings and that recognising this keeps one label from taking over after a hurtful remark.

passage: Sunday night. Strange week. At the Delhi university welcome, everyone called me "the Bombay girl," and I found myself defending vada pav as if my life depended on it. Tuesday, in the philosophy seminar, I was only a student fighting about free will; nobody cared where I came from. Thursday, at the badminton club, I was just Ira who smashes too hard. Friday, Pema from Gangtok and I sat on the hostel roof, and she said she felt more "northeastern" in Delhi than she ever did at home. Me too, with Mumbai. It's as if different parts of me step forward depending on who's in the room. Honestly, that's a relief. If someone squeezes me down to "the Bombay girl," I know it's one door, not the house. - Ira

passage: In the village near Akola, everyone called Vaibhav "the college boy" the moment he got off the bus with his agriculture textbooks. Uncles asked him about seed prices as if he were an expert. At the college hostel, it was the opposite: there he was "the farmer's son," the one who knew how cotton actually smelled. And on Sunday evenings at the kabaddi ground, he was simply the best raider on the left side. His cousin Indu laughed when he told her. "So which one are you?" Vaibhav, twenty, thought about it while they walked back past the well. "All of them. Whichever the people around me notice first." Last month a hostel senior had sneered at "village boys," and it had stung for days. Now it stung less. He was a village boy. He was also three other things.

qa.q: What did the uncles in the village ask Vaibhav about?
qa.a: They asked him about seed prices as if he were an expert.

qa.q: Why does the hostel senior's sneer sting Vaibhav less now?
qa.a: Because he has realised he is several things at once, so being called a village boy no longer feels like the whole of him.

qa.q: Which choice in how Vaibhav sees himself helps him, and why?
qa.a: It lets him own being a village boy with pride while knowing no single label, good or bad, gets to take over.

qa.a: Indu might see that Vaibhav changes a little depending on where he is, and that this is not being fake but having many true sides.

Then one afternoon a classmate made a joke about "people like her," and suddenly she felt only Moroccan, hot-faced and defensive. The next morning, in the lab, Tariq asked her about the bridge model, and she was an engineer again. Walking home, she realised no single label had the whole of her. That felt freeing.

passage: In the hostel at the engineering college in Warangal, Simran, nineteen, from Patna, was surprised how often she changed. At dinner, when a group mocked Bihari accents, she felt fiercely Bihari, suddenly using words she hadn't said in months. In the robotics lab, nobody cared where she came from; she was the one who knew the motor controls, and she felt like pure engineer. At the common-room TV on match nights, she was a cricket fan, yelling next to Mahima from Kerala. "You're like three different people," Mahima said. Simran laughed. "Maybe that's good." She thought of how, a year ago, she'd felt only Bihari, only an outsider, every day. Now, depending on who was in the room, other parts of her came forward. No single label could swallow her.

qa.q: What did Simran know in the robotics lab?
qa.a: She was the one who knew the motor controls.

qa.q: What did Simran feel at dinner when accents were mocked?
qa.a: Simran felt fiercely and defensively Bihari, stung by the mockery.

qa.q: Why is it useful for Simran to notice her many identities?
qa.a: It stops one label from taking over, so mockery of one part doesn't define all of her.

grounding: A student feels Bihari, engineer or cricket fan depending on who is present, and noticing this keeps any single label from taking over.

Dear Neelam didi,
You asked if Bengaluru has changed me. I think it's more that I've split into pieces, in a good way.
At the Tamil landlord's house, I'm "the Odia boy." At work in the start-up, I'm the backend guy, and nobody cares what I eat. On Sundays I play cricket in the park with a group from Kerala and Assam, and I'm just the slow bowler who can't field.
Last week in a meeting someone joked about Odias being "too quiet for sales." For a moment I was only Odia, angry and embarrassed. Then my manager asked for my database plan, and I was an engineer again.
Realising this helps. No single label gets to be all of me. Tell Maa I'm eating properly.
Harish

qa.a: Harish felt angry and embarrassed, as if he were only Odia in that moment.

passage: The Howrah train was delayed six hours, so Arnab spent the night at Bengaluru station with whoever else was stuck. At 11 pm, sharing a bench with a family from Kolkata, he was all Bengali, arguing about fish curry and the best sweet shop in Bhowanipore. At 1 am, when a group of engineering students from another college sat nearby, he was suddenly an engineer, debating circuits and complaining about exams. At 3 am the station TV showed a cricket replay, and he was just a fan, yelling with strangers from Kerala and Punjab. His classmate Binita, travelling with him, laughed. 'You've been three different people tonight.' Arnab thought about it. 'Maybe that's good. If I was only Bengali, I'd have spent the night alone.'

passage: In her Delhi law college, Farida felt like five people in one Tuesday. At the 9 am moot court she was a future lawyer, sharp and fast. At lunch with the Lucknow students she was a Lucknowi, teasing Delhi people about their manners. On the football ground she was a goalkeeper, nothing else. Then at the evening seminar on religion and law, every head turned to her when the professor asked for 'a Muslim perspective', and she felt the other four people vanish. Her classmate Siddharth caught her face afterwards. 'You looked annoyed.' 'I am. I'm a lot of things. In there I was only one.' He thought. 'I get it. At home I'm only the eldest son.' They walked to the metro together, a lawyer, a Lucknowi, a goalkeeper and her friend.

qa.q: What was Farida on the football ground?
qa.a: A goalkeeper, nothing else.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when every head turned to her in the seminar?
qa.a: Farida felt annoyed and resentful, reduced to a single label while the rest of her vanished.

qa.q: What could the professor have done differently?
qa.a: Invite views from anyone interested instead of turning to Farida as the representative, letting students speak as individuals.

It helped to see that no single label is all of me. Next time someone says "the Bihari one", I'll let it be one part, not the whole.
